strapline: A motion to redraw the ministries, the Cabinet question that will not go away, a K52.6 million FISP audit — and a Zambian first at Absa L'Atelier

stories.title: Redrawing the ministries before naming the ministers: Hichilema asks Parliament to approve the creation, merger and dissolution of ministries, with Nalumango to move the motion
stories.excerpt: State House said on Monday 26 October that President Hakainde Hichilema has written to the National Assembly under Article 92(2)(d) of the Constitution seeking approval for a realignment of government ministries, which it says will put the machinery of government behind the Grow Zambia Agenda. Vice-President Mutale Nalumango will move the motion. No ministry has yet been named, no date set, and the request lands with a Cabinet of four ministers two and a half months after the election.

image.label: Article 92(2)(d)
image.caption: State House announced on Monday 26 October 2026 that the President has asked Parliament to approve the establishment, merger and dissolution of ministries.

body: President Hakainde Hichilema has asked the National Assembly to approve a reorganisation of government ministries, State House announced on Monday 26 October. According to a press statement issued in Lusaka by the Chief Communications Specialist, Clayson Hamasaka, and reported by the Lusaka Times, News Diggers, Zambia Monitor, Open Zambia and the Zambian Observer, the President wrote to Parliament under Article 92(2)(d) of the Constitution, the provision under which the establishment, merger and dissolution of ministries requires the approval of the House.

The statement says the request is for the "proposed establishment, merger and dissolution of Government Ministries", and that the Vice-President, Mutale Nalumango, will move the motion on the floor of the House. Zambia Monitor quotes the statement as describing the exercise as a step to "realign Government Ministries as a measure to enhance the efficiency of Government". The Lusaka Times reports the stated aim as ensuring that "the machinery of Government fully supports the Grow Zambia Agenda", the economic programme of the President's second term, and improving public service delivery. The President, the statement adds, "has therefore called on Members of Parliament to support the realignment, which is in the best interest of the country."

None of the five reports names a single ministry to be created, merged or closed, and none gives a date for the debate. The Lusaka Times says those details are expected when the Vice-President tables the motion; Zambia Monitor says the proposal is expected to be debated in coming sittings. The Lusaka Times also sets out what normally follows parliamentary approval: ministers have to be appointed to any new ministries, staff moved across and budget lines redrawn, changes that would then show up in the national budget. The 2027 budget is due to be presented on Friday 30 October, as Lusaka Brief reported on Monday.

The same paper draws the contrast with 2021. Soon after taking office, the President created the Ministry of Green Economy and Environment, the Ministry of Technology and Science and the Ministry of Small and Medium Enterprise Development, and merged or dissolved others; Parliament took the matter up in September that year, after the event. This time, the Lusaka Times notes, approval is being sought before any change takes effect. It expects the ruling UPND to have the numbers to pass the motion, and expects opposition MPs to press on the cost of new ministries, on what happens to staff in merged or dissolved ones, and on whether service delivery will actually improve.

The request arrives while most ministries still have no substantive minister. The President was sworn in on 1 September after the 13 August election. On 14 September he swore in his first four ministers: Situmbeko Musokotwane, reappointed to Finance and National Planning; Mulambo Haimbe, returning to Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation; Gilbert Siame at Green Economy and Environment; and Roma Chilengi at Health, according to a report by Bénin Web TV. News Diggers reported on Monday that no further appointments have followed, and that some UPND officials have defended the delay on the ground that the Constitution sets no deadline for naming a Cabinet. Lusaka Brief reported on Friday 23 October that the President had re-appointed his seven presidential advisers while the Cabinet was still awaited; that remains the position. The debate over the delay, and the political scientist Neo Simutanyi's call for the ruling party to censure the President over it, is reported separately in this edition.

The Zambian Observer's account of the State House statement places the realignment in the context of the Grow Zambia targets the government has set itself: 10,000 MW of generation capacity, ten million tonnes of maize, five million tourists a year, three million tonnes of copper and US$1 billion in beef exports. Which ministries would carry which of those targets is the question the motion will have to answer.

body.title: What to watch
items: The text of the Vice-President's motion: which ministries are created, merged or dissolved
The date of the debate, and whether it comes before or after Friday's budget speech
Whether the full Cabinet is named once the new structure is approved
The cost: new ministries mean new ministers, permanent secretaries and budget lines

body.confirmed: That the President has written to Parliament under Article 92(2)(d) seeking approval for the establishment, merger and dissolution of ministries, that the Vice-President will move the motion, and that the stated purpose is efficiency and alignment with the Grow Zambia Agenda: State House statement of 26 October as reported by the Lusaka Times, News Diggers, Zambia Monitor, Open Zambia and the Zambian Observer. That four ministers were sworn in on 14 September: Bénin Web TV.
body.unverified: Which ministries are affected, how many there will be, what the changes will cost and when the House will debate the motion. None of this has been published. Suggested lists of ministries circulating in commentary, including one appended to the Zambian Observer's report, are the authors' proposals, not the government's.

stories.title: Censure him, do not defend him: Simutanyi tells the UPND to hold the President to account over a Cabinet of four, as party officials say the Constitution sets no deadline
stories.excerpt: The political scientist Neo Simutanyi says a government running on four ministers more than two months after the election is damaging governance and making Zambia a laughing stock, and that the ruling party should hold the President to account rather than explain the delay away. UPND officials have argued that the Constitution gives no timetable for Cabinet appointments. News Diggers and the Zambian Observer carried his remarks on Monday 26 October.

image.label: Four ministers
image.caption: Only four ministers have been appointed since the 13 August 2026 election; Neo Simutanyi says the ruling party should stop defending the delay.

body: The delay in appointing a full Cabinet drew its sharpest criticism yet on Monday 26 October, when the political scientist Dr Neo Simutanyi called on officials of the ruling UPND to stop justifying it and to censure President Hakainde Hichilema instead. News Diggers reported that Simutanyi believes the delay is affecting governance and making Zambia a laughing stock, and that the President has had enough time to identify qualified people for his administration. More than two months after the August general election, the paper noted, only four ministers have been appointed, and stakeholders have raised concerns about what the vacancies mean for the running of government.

The Zambian Observer carried a longer version of his remarks. In its account Simutanyi accused the President of concentrating power in his own hands, asked how ministries could function without substantive ministers, and asked whether the President intended to run those ministries himself. It quotes him as saying that "Zambia is today a laughing stock because of a President who is not serious with national affairs", and that the President "loves power too much".

body.text: Zambia is today a laughing stock because of a President who is not serious with national affairs.
body.attribution: Dr Neo Simutanyi, political scientist, as quoted by the Zambian Observer on Monday 26 October

body: Both papers report the UPND's defence: that the Constitution sets no deadline for the appointment of Cabinet ministers. Simutanyi's reply, as the Observer reports it, is that the absence of a deadline is not a reason for delay, and that party officials should demand accountability rather than defend the President as a matter of course. Neither report carries a response from State House or the party to Monday's remarks.

The four ministers in office are Situmbeko Musokotwane at Finance and National Planning, Mulambo Haimbe at Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, Gilbert Siame at Green Economy and Environment and Roma Chilengi at Health, all sworn in on 14 September, according to Bénin Web TV's report of the ceremony. Every other ministry is without a substantive minister.

The criticism landed on the day State House announced that the President has asked Parliament to approve the establishment, merger and dissolution of ministries, reported as the lead story in this edition. The Lusaka Times notes that new ministries normally require ministers to be appointed once they exist, which offers one possible explanation for the sequence the President has chosen: structure first, names second. No official has said so. The Observer's report has Simutanyi putting the interval at about four months; the election was held on 13 August and the President was sworn in on 1 September, which puts Monday's remarks a little under eleven weeks into the term.

stories.title: K52.6 million of inputs to inactive and double-dipping farmers: an agriculture foundation demands a FISP investigation after the Auditor-General's findings
stories.excerpt: The Agriculture Climate Action Foundation says the 2025 Auditor-General's report shows 2,128 inactive farmers were allocated K17.76 million of redeemable inputs and 4,213 beneficiaries got K34.92 million of inputs while already on other support programmes. It wants to know whether the failures were in the e-voucher or the direct supply system, and who will answer for them. A separate audit finding, reported last week, put K19.6 million of inputs in the hands of 2,339 farmers who were not on the national register.

image.label: K52.6 million
image.caption: ACAF wants the Ministry of Agriculture to explain K52.6 million of FISP input irregularities identified in the 2025 Auditor-General's report.

body: The Agriculture Climate Action Foundation Zambia (ACAF) has called for an investigation into irregularities worth K52.6 million in the Farmer Input Support Programme identified in the 2025 report of the Auditor-General, The Mast reported on Monday 26 October. According to the paper, the foundation's executive director, Dr Oliver Bulaya, cited two findings: that 2,128 inactive farmers were allocated redeemable inputs worth K17.76 million, and that 4,213 beneficiaries received inputs worth K34.92 million despite already benefiting from other government support programmes.

Bulaya is quoted as saying the findings "raise serious questions about the integrity, transparency, and effectiveness of the systems" used to run the programme. He asked the government to say whether the irregularities arose under the e-voucher system or the Direct Input Supply system, arguing that "if these irregularities occurred under the E-voucher system, the effectiveness of its verification, monitoring, and control mechanisms must be critically reviewed". He asked who was responsible, what action would follow, and why the discrepancies were not caught before public money was put at risk.

body.text: Every kwacha lost through irregularities represents resources that could otherwise support genuine farmers.
body.attribution: Dr Oliver Bulaya, executive director, Agriculture Climate Action Foundation Zambia, in a statement reported by The Mast on Monday 26 October

body: The Mast reports that the foundation is asking the Ministry of Agriculture and oversight institutions for a comprehensive review of FISP, including independent verification of beneficiaries, investigations and the recovery of funds where the law allows, with administrative or legal action against anyone found responsible, through due process. Bulaya also suggested that the government consider using qualified, independent private-sector providers for beneficiary registration and verification, programme administration and input delivery and monitoring, while the state keeps control of policy, financing, eligibility criteria and regulation. The paper carries no response from the Ministry of Agriculture.

The findings sit alongside another from the same audit cycle. The Zambian Observer reported on Wednesday 21 October that the Auditor-General found 2,339 farmers whose details could not be traced on the authorised national farmer register had accessed inputs worth more than K19.6 million in the 2025/26 season: 1,343 in Isoka, with inputs valued at over K11.2 million; 995 in Mpika, over K8.3 million; and one in Mansa, worth K8,200. The Observer's report, like The Mast's, carries no ministry response.

The programme the audit describes is the one now being rolled out for a new season. Lusaka Brief reported on Monday that the Ministry of Agriculture had put the number of farmers who have redeemed their 2026/27 inputs at 675,459, about two-thirds of the target. The Auditor-General's figures concern the previous season; whether the controls have changed since is the question ACAF's statement puts to the ministry.

stories.title: A K2.2 billion test of appetite the day before the budget: Access Bank says Thursday's Treasury bill auction will show what investors think of the government's borrowing
stories.excerpt: The Bank of Zambia offers K2.2 billion of Treasury bills on Thursday 29 October, the day before the 2027 budget is read, with a third of the paper at one year. Access Bank's market note says FISP and Food Reserve Agency payments are about to push kwacha into rural areas, that the maize stockpile is prudent but expensive, and that 2027 is the risk year if the rains fail. On the stock exchange, a quiet week saw CEC account for almost half of turnover.

image.label: Thursday 29 October
image.caption: A K2.2 billion Treasury bill auction settles on 2 November 2026, days after the 2027 budget is presented to Parliament.

body: The last market event before Friday's budget speech is a Treasury bill auction. Zambia Monitor reported on Monday 26 October, citing a market commentary from Access Bank, that the Bank of Zambia will offer K2.2 billion of bills, about US$109 million, on Thursday 29 October, for settlement on Monday 2 November. The offer is split across four tenors: K440 million at 91 days, K500 million at 182 days, K530 million at 273 days and K730 million at 364 days, so that roughly a third of the paper is one-year money.

The bank's note, as Zambia Monitor reports it, frames the sale as a gauge of investor appetite for government debt at a time when the authorities are preparing a supplementary budget. Lusaka Brief reported on Friday 23 October that the Finance Minister has asked Parliament for K19.9 billion more for 2026, most of it to pay farmers for maize bought by the Food Reserve Agency, and that most of the extra spending is to be met by domestic borrowing. Access Bank says investors will be watching the bid-to-cover ratios and the yields accepted at the auction.

The commentary makes three further points. Payments under the Farmer Input Support Programme and to the Food Reserve Agency are about to inject kwacha liquidity into rural areas, which, depending on how they are financed, could expand the money supply and put marginal pressure on the currency. The decision to stockpile food after a strong harvest is, in the bank's words as reported, prudent, and should keep inflation subdued in the near term, but it adds to the strain on public finances at a time when growth expectations are being revised down. And the main risk period is 2027: an unfavourable rainy season would cut agricultural output, electricity generation and growth at the same time. The Government activated its El Niño preparedness plan last week, as Lusaka Brief reported on Sunday.

body.text: A thin week on the exchange

body: On the Lusaka Securities Exchange, The Mast reported, citing the Stockbrokers Zambia weekly equity and economic report, that turnover for the week of 9 to 16 October fell to K2.17 million on 490,591 shares, from K5.38 million on 672,307 shares the week before. CEC Plc accounted for 46.37 per cent of turnover, just over K1 million, with Airtel Networks Zambia second. Dot Com Zambia led the gainers, up 11.79 per cent to K27.50; Zanaco slipped 0.22 per cent to K8.95, and Zambia Sugar and Chilanga Cement closed marginally lower at K67.99 and K60.98. The Mast notes that CEC's share price had drifted down to K15.01 by 21 October, and attributes part of the decline to the kwacha's appreciation over the year to the third quarter, since the company earns mostly in US dollars; it reports the Securities and Exchange Commission as describing price fluctuations on the exchange as normal.

The sequence for the week is therefore the auction on Thursday, the budget on Friday and settlement on Monday, by which time the market will know both the price investors put on the government's paper and the size of the borrowing requirement the Finance Minister intends to put before them in 2027.

stories.title: 4,509,005 children to reach in a week: Chilengi launches Child Health Week and says the services should be routine, not an annual campaign
stories.excerpt: The Minister of Health, Professor Roma Chilengi, launched the 2026 Child Health Week in Lusaka on Monday 26 October with a target of more than 4.5 million under-fives for vitamin A, deworming, nutrition screening and catch-up immunisation, and HPV vaccination for girls of nine. The Ministry estimates that about one child in five missed a life-saving vaccine before its first birthday. World Vision moved 900,000 vitamin A doses and nearly four million deworming tablets to the provinces.

image.label: Child Health Week
image.caption: The 2026 Child Health Week, launched on Monday 26 October 2026, targets 4,509,005 children under five across Zambia.

body: The 2026 Child Health Week was launched in Lusaka on Monday 26 October by the Minister of Health, Professor Roma Chilengi, with a national target of 4,509,005 children under five, Zambia Monitor reported. The week-long campaign offers vitamin A supplementation, deworming, mid-upper arm circumference screening for malnutrition, routine and catch-up immunisation and, for eligible girls aged nine, the HPV vaccine against cervical cancer. The theme, according to the same report, is "Strengthening Community Health Systems: Closing the Last Mile for Every Child".

The Lusaka Times gives the age bands: vitamin A for children of six to 59 months, deworming from twelve to 59 months, and nutrition screening from six to 59 months. It reports that the Ministry estimates about one in five children missed a critical vaccine before their first birthday, and that under-five mortality now stands at 42 deaths per 1,000 live births. The campaign is aimed at children who missed scheduled interventions, particularly in rural and remote communities, and at those Zambia Monitor describes the Minister as calling underserved for geographical, socio-economic, cultural or health-system reasons.

body.text: Strengthening Community Health Systems: Closing the Last Mile for Every Child
body.attribution: Theme of the 2026 Child Health Week, as reported by Zambia Monitor on Monday 26 October

body: Chilengi used the launch to argue that the services on offer should not depend on an annual push. The Lusaka Times reports him calling for a shift from campaigns to "routine delivery of essential healthcare services to ensure that no child is left behind", with immunisation, vitamin A, deworming and screening becoming part of daily health care. Zambia Monitor quotes him describing the week as "a strategic public health intervention" and linking children's health to human capital, educational attainment and long-term development.

The launch was attended by the Ministry's permanent secretaries, the UNICEF country representative, Dr Saja Farooq Abdullah, and the WHO country representative, Dr Peter Clement Lasuba, according to Zambia Monitor. The Lusaka Times reports Abdullah saying UNICEF would continue to support immunisation, breastfeeding promotion, nutrition and vitamin A supplementation, and the roll-out of the integrated reproductive, maternal, newborn, child and nutrition outreach package. World Vision Zambia transported the supplies to all provincial centres before distribution to facilities: about 900,000 vitamin A supplements and nearly four million deworming tablets, its strategy, impact and learning director, Ekwase Msoni, is quoted as saying.

Neither report gives the closing date of the week, the launch venue or a provincial breakdown of the target. The campaign runs while the country is also managing a cholera outbreak, reported separately in this edition; neither launch report mentions it.

stories.title: Past 1,300 cases and 27 deaths: the cholera outbreak has reached 18 districts in six provinces, with Lusaka carrying more than half the count and Chibombo most of the rest
stories.excerpt: The Mast reports a ZNPHI update showing 53 new cases and one death in a day, taking the outbreak to 1,314 cumulative cases, 27 deaths and 1,233 recoveries, with 54 patients in hospital. Lusaka has 723 cases and Chibombo 272. A later tally carried by Outbreak News Today on Monday 26 October put the count at 1,488 cases and 29 deaths, a figure Lusaka Brief has not been able to match to a published ZNPHI bulletin.

image.label: 18 districts, six provinces
image.caption: ZNPHI figures reported by The Mast put the cholera outbreak at 1,314 cases and 27 deaths; a later tally reported 1,488 and 29.

body: Zambia's cholera outbreak has spread to 18 districts in six provinces, with 1,314 cumulative cases and 27 deaths, according to a Zambia National Public Health Institute update reported by The Mast on Monday 26 October. The update recorded 53 new cases in 24 hours, four of them laboratory-confirmed, and one new death. The paper reports 1,233 patients as recovered and discharged and 54 in hospital. The ZNPHI is quoted as saying that "cumulative deaths have risen to 27, with 1,233 patients having recovered and been discharged" and that "the outbreak has spread across 18 districts in six provinces".

Lusaka District remains the centre of the outbreak with 723 cases, about 55 per cent of the national total. Chibombo has 272, Chongwe 71, Chienge 56, Chilanga 46, Mwansabombwe 39 and Mpulungu 38, according to the district figures The Mast reproduces. The Mast dates the start of the outbreak to 28 July; the Ministry of Health's formal declaration came on 30 September, when, as Lusaka Brief reported on 2 October, there were 304 cases and 11 deaths in seven districts across five provinces. The count has more than quadrupled in four weeks.

A tally published by Outbreak News Today on Monday 26 October gives higher numbers: 1,488 cumulative cases, 219 of them confirmed, 29 deaths, 68 new cases in the previous 24 hours, and 845 cases in Lusaka, about 57 per cent of the total, across the same 18 districts and six provinces. That report does not name its source, and Lusaka Brief has not found a published ZNPHI bulletin with those figures. The two accounts agree on the geographic spread and on Lusaka's share; they differ by 174 cases and two deaths, which is consistent with updates issued on different days but cannot be confirmed from what has been published.

body.title: Cumulative cases by district, as reported by The Mast

body: The ZNPHI's advice, as reported, is unchanged: wash hands with soap and water, drink boiled or treated water, cook food thoroughly, keep toilets clean, and take anyone with watery diarrhoea or vomiting to the nearest health facility at once. The Child Health Week launched on Monday, reported separately in this edition, will put outreach teams into the same districts over the coming days.

body.confirmed: 1,314 cumulative cases, 27 deaths, 1,233 discharged, 54 in hospital, 53 new cases and one death in a day, 18 districts in six provinces, Lusaka 723 and Chibombo 272: ZNPHI update as reported by The Mast. Declaration on 30 September with 304 cases: Lusaka Brief's coverage of 2 October.
body.unverified: The figure of 1,488 cases and 29 deaths published by Outbreak News Today, which names no source, and the date each set of figures refers to.

stories.title: 'The State is not ready to prosecute': Mundubile, Zulu and 16 others argue that investigating after charge cannot justify holding them, a day before their bail hearing resumes
stories.excerpt: In arguments reported by News Diggers on Monday 26 October, the 18 accused in the treason case say the State has admitted it is still investigating after charging them, that this shows it is not ready to prosecute, and that their detention breaches their constitutional rights. Their application for constitutional bail is due back before a three-judge High Court panel at 09:00 on Wednesday 28 October, when the court has directed that all 18 be produced.

image.label: Wednesday, 09:00
image.caption: The constitutional bail application by Brian Mundubile, Makebi Zulu and 16 others returns to a three-judge High Court panel on 28 October 2026.

body: Brian Mundubile, Makebi Zulu and 16 co-accused have told the High Court that they should be released on constitutional bail because the State, by its own account, is still investigating them after charging them with treason, News Diggers reported on Monday 26 October. According to the paper, the 18 argue that the State cannot rely on continuing investigations to hold them indefinitely without trial, that this amounts to an admission that it is not ready to prosecute, and that their detention violates their constitutional rights. They have also sued the Attorney-General, Mulilo Kabesha, over alleged breaches of their rights while in custody.

The application is due back in court on Wednesday 28 October at 09:00. Zambia Monitor reported on Thursday 22 October that the previous sitting, before a panel of Ndola High Court Judge Derrick Mulenga and Justices Davies Chibwili and Ireen Wishimanga, did not reach the merits. Preliminary issues raised by the State stalled the proceedings; the two sides then agreed by consent to join the Director of Public Prosecutions, Gilbert Phiri, as a respondent and to remove two officials who had been sued personally, the head of the Anti-Fraud and Cyber Crime Unit, Harrington Akushanga, and the Commissioner-General of the Correctional Service, Frederick Chilukutu.

Zambia Monitor reported the Attorney-General as telling reporters after the chamber hearing that the two officials had been performing official duties and had not been served, and that the DPP was joined because the application arose from criminal proceedings. Phiri was to be served with the application and arguments once the consent order was filed, with no deadline set for his response. The defence, led by Sakwiba Sikota, said the accused had conceded the State's preliminary points to avoid further delay, but the State still asked for more time. The defence also complained that the 18 had not been brought to court, leaving counsel unable to take final instructions; the State gave no reason for their absence and the court directed that they be produced on Wednesday.

The accused, who include the former Anglican bishop Trevor Mwamba, are held at Mukobeko Maximum Security Prison and face charges including treason and offences relating to terrorism and sedition, according to Zambia Monitor. They allege that they were not brought before a competent court for about two months after their apprehension. News Diggers' report refers to an arrest over allegations concerning the possession of high-grade military material; the detail of that allegation, and the State's written answer to Monday's arguments, were not available in the published text.

body.confirmed: That 18 accused including Mundubile and Zulu have applied for constitutional bail; that the application returns to a three-judge panel at 09:00 on 28 October with the accused to be produced; that the DPP has been joined and two officials removed by consent; and the charges as described: Zambia Monitor, 22 October. The accused's argument that continuing investigation shows the State is not ready to prosecute: News Diggers, 26 October.
body.unverified: The State's response to the arguments reported on Monday, whether the panel will rule on Wednesday, and the substance of the allegations against the 18, which have not been tested in court. All 18 are presumed innocent.

stories.title: 'Don't look down on yourselves, girls': Kanyemba calls the U-17 World Cup bad for Zambia, apologises to the fans and says the Copper Princesses need far more games at this level
stories.excerpt: Carol Kanyemba's review of a tournament that ended with three defeats, two goals scored and nine conceded is unsparing: a setback on the last edition, returning players who did not repeat their form, and a gap between African and World Cup level that only exposure can close. She says selection and scouting will be reviewed and that the U-20 and senior teams are already looking at the graduating players. ZamFoot and News Diggers carried her remarks.

image.label: Three games, no points
image.caption: Zambia lost 5–0 to Japan, 3–2 to Venezuela and 1–0 to France at the FIFA U-17 Women's World Cup in Morocco.

body: Carol Kanyemba has described the Copper Princesses' FIFA U-17 Women's World Cup as "bad for us", a tournament in Morocco from which Zambia returned without a point after losing 5–0 to Japan, 3–2 to Venezuela and 1–0 to France in Group D. ZamFoot reported her review on Sunday 25 October and News Diggers followed on Monday 26 October with her post-match remarks after the France game, which Lusaka Brief reported on Sunday.

Her assessment, as ZamFoot reports it, is that failing to collect a point was a setback compared with Zambia's previous appearance, and that while the under-17 level is developmental, players still have to learn how to win if they are to make the transition to senior football. Some of the squad were returning from the last edition and others were debutants; some of the returning players, she said, did not reproduce their earlier form, and players develop at different rates. She pointed out that the team had gone through six qualifiers unbeaten to get to Morocco and had shown character in doing so.

body.text: The gap and how to close it

body: The central point in both reports is exposure. ZamFoot quotes her saying the distance between African and World Cup level means the team needs to be exposed more; News Diggers' headline has her saying the Copper Princesses need more international exposure to compete at World Cup level. She praised the players' resilience and their achievement in qualifying. News Diggers quotes her: "First and foremost, I want to appreciate all the efforts that they put in."

body.text: Don't look down on yourselves, girls. You've got this, and you are as good as everyone else.
body.attribution: Carol Kanyemba, Copper Princesses head coach, to her players after the U-17 Women's World Cup, as reported by ZamFoot on Sunday 25 October

body: On what happens next, ZamFoot reports that the technical bench will review its selection and scouting processes, continue developing both the players who remain eligible at under-17 level and those who graduate, and keep scouting to fill the gaps the graduates leave. The under-20 and senior national teams are already targeting some of the departing players, she said. She apologised to supporters and said criticism helps the coaching staff improve.

Kanyemba's tournament ended with a national honour as well as three defeats. She was awarded the President's Insignia of Meritorious Achievement at the Independence Day investiture on 24 October, as Lusaka Brief reported on Monday, in recognition of taking Zambia to three consecutive under-17 World Cups.

stories.title: Five pieces that survived a flooded studio: Emmanuel Chisenga, 24, of Lusaka becomes the first Zambian to win an Absa L'Atelier Ambassador Award
stories.excerpt: Chisenga, a business administration student with no formal art training, shares the 2026 Ambassador Award with Reginald Boateng of Ghana and Segun Owolabi of Nigeria in the competition's 40th year. The prize is a solo exhibition, R100,000 towards materials, masterclasses and a four-month mentorship. Zambia Monitor reports it as the first nomination and win for Zambia since the group structure was introduced in 2019.

image.label: A Zambian first
image.caption: Emmanuel Chisenga of Lusaka won an Ambassador Award at the 2026 Absa L'Atelier Art Competition, the first Zambian to do so.

body: Emmanuel Chisenga, a 24-year-old artist from Lusaka, has won an Ambassador Award at the 2026 Absa L'Atelier Art Competition, the first Zambian to take one of the continental competition's top prizes. Zambia Monitor reported the win on Monday 26 October; the winners were announced on a Saturday at the Absa L'Atelier Art and Lifestyle Fair at Waterfall City Park in South Africa, the weekend before the Sowetan's report of Tuesday 13 October.

Chisenga did not come to art through a school. Zambia Monitor quotes him: "I didn't follow a traditional path into the world of art by learning it in school." He is studying for a Bachelor of Business Administration and is the youngest of four children. The Sowetan reports that the five pieces he submitted were what remained after flooding destroyed his studio, and quotes him on the win: "This art is not much, but it's life changing." Being the first Zambian winner, he told the paper, is a huge responsibility, because people are now looking up to him.

body.text: This art is not much, but it's life changing.
body.attribution: Emmanuel Chisenga, Absa L'Atelier Ambassador Award winner, as quoted by the Sowetan on 13 October

body: Absa L'Atelier was established in 1986 and runs in partnership with the South African National Association for the Visual Arts; this was its 40th year. Zambia Monitor reports that hundreds of eligible entries came from twelve Absa markets in Africa and were assessed by an independent panel, and that Chisenga's is the first nomination and the first win for Zambia since the group structure was introduced in 2019. The Ambassador Award, according to the Sowetan, brings a solo exhibition, R100,000 towards material costs, art masterclasses and a four-month mentorship with a leading visual-arts figure from the winner's country.

He shares the award with Reginald Boateng, 27, a Ghanaian photographer and environmental activist whose piece "Our Water Turns Red" addresses illegal gold mining, and Segun Owolabi, 27, a Nigerian painter who makes portraits in thread. The Gerard Sekoto Award, the top honour for a South African artist, went to Treasure Mlima, 27, a self-taught wood carver from Durban, and carries a three-month residency at the Cité Internationale des Arts in Paris from April to June 2027. Dr Paul Bayliss, Absa's senior specialist in art and museum curator, is quoted by Zambia Monitor as saying that "the calibre of talent in this year's competition was exceptional".
Neither report describes the medium or subject of Chisenga's winning work, and neither gives the date or venue of his solo exhibition.

stories.title: Five presidents on the page and one missing: the Zambia Daily Mail issues an 'unreserved apology to the nation' for leaving the late Edgar Lungu out of its Independence supplement
stories.excerpt: The daily's 62nd anniversary supplement showed President Hichilema with Kaunda, Chiluba, Mwanawasa, Banda and Sata, and no Lungu. After a former Chienge MP demanded an explanation and social-media criticism built over the weekend, the company said the omission was entirely unintentional and is being handled administratively. The Zambian Observer reported the complaint on Saturday and the apology on Monday.

image.label: The missing sixth
image.caption: The Zambia Daily Mail apologised on Monday 26 October 2026 for omitting the late President Edgar Lungu from its Independence anniversary supplement.

body: Zambia Daily Mail Limited has apologised for leaving the late sixth President, Edgar Chagwa Lungu, out of its 62nd Independence anniversary supplement, the Zambian Observer reported on Monday 26 October. In a public notice reproduced in part by the Observer, the company said the omission "was entirely unintentional", offered an "unreserved apology to the nation", and said that management "regards this lapse with the seriousness it deserves, and the matter is being handled administratively". The Observer does not say who signed the notice.

The supplement, published on Friday 23 October, carried a commemorative page showing President Hakainde Hichilema alongside former presidents Kenneth Kaunda, Frederick Chiluba, Levy Mwanawasa, Rupiah Banda and Michael Sata, according to the Observer's earlier report of Saturday 24 October. Lungu, who governed from 2015 to 2021, was not on it. The Observer reported at the time that the reason for the exclusion was unclear and that the paper had not responded.

The first public objection the Observer recorded came from Given Katuta Mwelwa, the former Member of Parliament for Chienge, who asked the Daily Mail's management to explain the omission and take corrective action. "We cannot build a united Zambia by selectively remembering our history," she is quoted as saying, arguing that Independence Day should recognise every former head of state regardless of political affiliation. The Observer reported that the omission also drew criticism on social media, and that reaction among its own readers was divided, with some defending the page and others calling Lungu's presidency a matter of historical record.

body.text: We cannot build a united Zambia by selectively remembering our history.
body.attribution: Given Katuta Mwelwa, former MP for Chienge, as quoted by the Zambian Observer on Saturday 24 October

body: The apology leaves two questions the Observer's reports do not answer: how a commemorative page of presidents came to omit one, and what the administrative handling will consist of. Neither report carries a comment from the Lungu family or from the government. This account rests on the Observer's two reports; the Daily Mail's notice itself was not available online at the time of writing.

analysis.title: Structure before names: what the ministries motion does and does not settle
analysis.body: Article 92(2)(d) makes Parliament the gatekeeper for the shape of government, and the President has chosen to go through that gate before filling the offices behind it. That answers one criticism of 2021, when new ministries were created first and approved afterwards, and it offers an explanation for a Cabinet of four that no official has yet given aloud: that ministers are not being named for ministries that may not exist in a month. It does not answer the question Neo Simutanyi and others are asking, which is why the sequence has taken eleven weeks, nor the one opposition MPs will put in the debate, which is what the new structure costs. The strongest case for the government is that a second-term programme built around specific production targets needs ministries drawn to match them. The strongest case against is that ministries can be redrawn in a week and ministers appointed in a day, and the country has had neither. What to watch: the list of ministries, the date of the debate relative to Friday's budget, and how quickly the names follow the structure.

analysis.title: The audit figures arrive just as the next season's inputs go out
analysis.body: Three separate findings from the Auditor-General's latest cycle now concern FISP: K17.76 million of inputs to inactive farmers, K34.92 million to beneficiaries already on other programmes, and K19.6 million to farmers not on the national register, concentrated in Isoka and Mpika. Together they describe a verification problem rather than a theft problem, which is why ACAF's question about whether the failures sit in the e-voucher or the direct supply channel matters: the two systems have different controls and different points of failure. The ministry has not yet responded to either report. Against that is a programme that is, by the ministry's own figures, two-thirds redeemed for 2026/27 and ahead of last year's pace, and a Finance Ministry that has just asked for K19.9 billion more largely to pay for the maize that last year's inputs produced. The budget on Friday will show whether FISP is funded at this year's cost or last year's plan. What is not known is whether the register has been cleaned between the audited season and this one.

analysis.title: Wednesday's hearing turns on a timing argument the court has not yet reached
analysis.body: The bail application by the 18 treason accused has been adjourned more than once without a ruling on its substance, and Wednesday's sitting is the first at which the merits can be heard with the parties the court has now settled on. The accused's argument, as reported, is a narrow one: that a State which is still investigating after charging has conceded it cannot yet try them, and that detention cannot be justified by an investigation with no end date. The State's position at the last sitting, as reported, was about who had properly been sued, not about delay, and its answer on the merits has not yet been published. Both positions are arguable, and the panel may decide procedure before it decides liberty. What to watch: whether all 18 are produced as directed, whether the DPP files a response, and whether the court rules on Wednesday or reserves. None of it bears on guilt; the charges have not been tested and every one of the accused is presumed innocent.
